An 82-year-old man presented with painless right testicular swelling of several weeks’ duration without systemic symptoms. His history included glaucoma, prostatic adenomectomy, and hernioplasty; medications were dorzolamide, lansoprazole, and dutasteride. Testicular ultrasound showed enlargement and inhomogeneity of the right testis and epididymis with ipsilateral hydrocele. After 10 days of amoxicillin–clavulanate for presumed orchiepididymitis, swelling persisted. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirmed testicular pathology and revealed new bilateral macronodular adrenal enlargement measuring 15×12 mm on the right and 27×18 mm on the left, with homogeneous attenuation; these nodules were absent on a CT scan 3 years earlier. An 18 FDG PET/CT showed intense uptake (SUVmax 25.5) in the right testis but no uptake in the adrenal glands. Laboratory evaluation revealed normal electrolytes, blood count, iron studies, protein electrophoresis, glucose, renal and liver function, thyroid profile, LDH, and β2-microglobulin. Serologies were negative for active HCV and EBV (positive for past EBV). Clinically, he had no asthenia, headaches, abdominal pain, striae, or “buffalo hump,” and his blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg without hypertensive peaks on 24-hour monitoring.

A 19-month-old boy was brought to the emergency department after an episode of reduced consciousness while bathing. His parents reported that when lukewarm water was poured over his chest, he turned blue around the lips and began gasping for air. During this time, his eyes “rolled back,” and he did not interact with his parents. There were no clonic movements, and he did not respond to physical stimulation. He subsequently fell asleep for approximately 1 hour and was brought to the ED.

On arrival, he was alert and appeared well. There were no focal findings on examination, his development was appropriate, and laboratory studies—including a blood glucose level of 5.5 mmol/L—were normal. His parents reported similar, less profound episodes during bathing over the previous 2 weeks, in which his head would go back, his eyes would roll upward, and he would become floppy and limp for 2–3 minutes, followed by sleepiness. These episodes occurred only during bathing; contact with water in other settings did not provoke symptoms. He had normal developmental milestones and no significant past medical or family history.

An electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm with a normal QT interval. Bathing in lukewarm water while his vital signs were monitored provoked hypotonia, tachycardia, and brief apnea with associated desaturation. He stared straight ahead and made mouthing movements; he was removed from the bath, given high-flow oxygen, and again slept for about 1 hour. A further similar episode occurred later while he was sleeping, without any provocation. The first interictal EEG was normal using the standard 10–20 system. Because he was clinically well between episodes and there was an avoidable trigger, he was discharged with plans for follow-up investigations, including a brain MRI, a bathing EEG, and outpatient review.

On examination, percussion of both teeth was tender, and slight mobility was noted, but the overlying mucosa and skin were normal with no erythema, ulceration, or warmth. Intraoral palpation revealed bony‐hard consistency of the buccal and lingual cortices, and the mucosal integrity was intact.

An initial orthopantomogram showed a unilocular radiolucent lesion engulfing the apices of the right mandibular second premolar and a previously endodontically treated first molar, extending to the superior border of the inferior alveolar nerve canal; its irregular shape was atypical for routine periapical cysts or granulomas. Cone beam CT further demonstrated buccolingual expansion with almost complete obliteration of the lingual cortex, measuring approximately 23.4 × 14.2 × 6.6 mm.

Based on the radiographic findings, the preliminary differential diagnosis included odontogenic keratocyst, radicular cyst, and unicystic ameloblastoma.

An 83-year-old man presented with 6 months of progressive right mandibular pain radiating to the zygomatic and mastoid regions, requiring oxycodone, paracetamol, and ketorolac for relief. An empirical course of prednisone (50 mg per day) for presumed trigeminal neuralgia provided no benefit. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial CT showed enlargement of the right sphenoid sinus with overdevelopment and opacity of the lateral recess, bone thickening and sclerosis of the sphenoid walls, pterygoid process, and orbital apex, and focal interruption of the foramen rotundum and lateral recess wall. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI demonstrated soft tissue protruding through a breach in the lateral recess wall of the sphenoid sinus, invading the right internal pterygoid muscles, masticatory and pterygopalatine fossae, and infiltrating the V2 and V3 trigeminal branches; intracranial extension into the cavernous sinus surrounded the Gasserian ganglion, with the cavernous carotid artery patent. T2-weighted images showed a markedly hypointense signal in the lateral recess with peripheral mucosal inflammation. Endoscopic evaluation revealed purulent discharge in the sphenoethmoidal recess. The patient underwent right endoscopic sinus surgery: after middle turbinectomy, the sphenoid ostium was obstructed by a pyocele, which was marsupialized and drained; samples of the lesion and surrounding mucosa were sent for bacteriological and histopathological examination. The maxillary and ethmoid sinuses were then opened, the breach in the posterior-lateral sphenoid wall was repaired with mucoperiosteum, and a Merocel sponge was placed. He was discharged after 2 days without complications. Histopathology was negative for hyphae and neoplastic cells, and cultures grew no bacteria or fungi. One month after surgery, follow-up MRI confirmed persistent inflammation of the sphenoid sinus, skull base, and pterygoid fossa. A consultation with an infectious diseases specialist was sought.

A 34‐year‐old African American man with hemophilia A, HIV‐1 infection, and hepatitis C virus infection presented with a 3‐month history of intermittent fever, unintentional weight loss, and progressive lip swelling with painful ulcerations. Six months earlier he had resumed antiretroviral therapy, with his CD4 count rising from 94 to 160 cells/mm3; the lip lesions developed approximately two months after the CD4 count began to improve. He had received multiple courses of antibiotics and systemic corticosteroids without benefit. He was taking acyclovir for herpes simplex prophylaxis and dapsone for Pneumocystis jiroveci prophylaxis. 

On examination, his lips were markedly edematous, with multiple superficial ulcers having heaped‐up margins. There was no hepatosplenomegaly. The initial differential diagnosis included herpetic ulcers, bacterial infection, fungal infection, and angioedema. 

Diagnostic studies showed an undetectable HIV viral load and undetectable hepatitis C viral load. A polymerase‐chain‐reaction assay for herpes simplex virus from an ulcer base was negative. Complement C1 esterase inhibitor levels were within normal limits. Gram stain, acid‐fast stain, and mucicarmine stain of lesion samples were negative. Fungal blood cultures and both urine and serum Histoplasma antigen tests were negative.

A 71-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and ischemic heart disease presented with a 2-month history of intermittent painless hematuria with passage of clots. She denied dysuria, frequency, or other lower urinary tract symptoms, and there was no family history of malignancy. On examination, vital signs and abdominal and pelvic exams were unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation showed a hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL requiring blood transfusion; serum creatinine and other biochemical parameters were within normal limits. Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a 2.9 × 2.5 × 2.4 cm polypoidal mass arising from the posterolateral wall of the bladder dome; both kidneys and the upper tracts appeared normal. Pre- and postvoid bladder volumes were 180 mL and 44 mL, respectively. Cystoscopy demonstrated an exophytic solid tumor measuring 1.5 × 2.0 cm on the anterior fundal wall, covered with slough. A deep transurethral resection of the bladder tumor was performed. Histopathological analysis revealed an adenocarcinoma composed of mucinous and signet-ring cell components. Thus, a secondary adenocarcinoma or a rare variant of primary adenocarcinoma of the bladder was suspected.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Primary signet-ring cell carcinoma of the bladder
